title: Public Interest Litigation
lead: ==‘PIL is a constitutional instrument to make justice accessible and governance accountable’ — Justice P.N. Bhagwati, S.P. Gupta (1982).== PIL was first used by the SC in [[Fertilizer Corp. Kamgar Union v. UoI]].

head: Feature
Details
rows: ==Liberalisation of locus standi==
Anyone can file for others' rights — [[S.P. Gupta v. UoI (1982)]].
==Epistolary jurisdiction==

Letters or postcards treated as writ petitions ([[Sunil Batra]], [[Bandhua Mukti Morcha]]) — but the SC in ==[[Balwant Singh (2010)]]== restricted it to specific categories: bonded labour, children, environment, tribe & caste issues, women, police brutality.
==Non-adversarial nature==
Cooperative rather than combative — seeks ==social justice, not personal victory== ([[PUDR v. UoI, 1982]]).
Appointment of commissions
Courts may appoint ==expert commissions for fact-finding== ([[Sheela Barse v. State of MH]]).
==Judicial creativity==
New rights read into existing FRs — ==right to livelihood under Art 21== ([[Olga Tellis, 1985]]).
Flexibility in procedure
No rigid format — letters, telegrams, even emails accepted.
==Focus on group rights==
From individual grievances to ==community and environmental justice==.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages / Misuse
rows: ==Access to justice for marginalised sections==
==Frivolous PILs== for publicity or political motives ([[Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, 1991]])
Strengthens rule of law and participatory democracy
==Judicial overreach== into the policy domain ([[SCBA v. UoI, 1998]])
==Fills legislative or executive vacuum== (Vishaka Guidelines)
==Resource and time drain== — delays genuine cases
Encourages transparency, good governance, accountability
Used as a tool for ==blackmail or settling personal scores== ([[Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of WB, 2004]])
Promotes social change — women's rights, environment, education
==Middle-class capture== — shifting focus from the poor to civic and lifestyle issues

items.title: On Democracy
bullets: Strengthened judicial accountability and ==citizen participation in governance==
[[Vineet Narain v. UoI (1997)]] — led to ==CBI autonomy==
[[Common Cause v. UoI (2018)]] — transparency in governance and resource allocation

items.title: On Rights
bullets: ==Expanded Art 21==: education — [[Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993)]]
Shelter, food, health — [[PUCL v. UoI (Right to Food, 2001)]]

items.title: On the Power of Courts
bullets: Judiciary as ==policy enforcer and guardian of governance ethics==
Created ==green benches, vigilance commissions==, and guidelines absent legislation (Vishaka, 1997)

blocks.text: ==Prof. Upendra Baxi's distinction==: US PIL represents ==‘interests without groups’== (like consumerism); Indian ==Social Action Litigation (SAL)== represents ==‘interests within groups’== — focused on marginalised classes.

items: ==Ensure bona fide intent== — genuine public causes, not private interest
==Focus on implementation== — monitor compliance via committees or ==amicus curiae==
==Encourage institutional remedies== — use PILs to strengthen NHRC, NGT etc.
==Develop community litigation== — legal literacy and paralegal training
==Follow SC guidelines== — the 1988 and 2010 circulars on eligible categories
==Digital PILs== — the SC's post-2021 e-Filing and PIL Portal
==Collaborations== between civil society, media and judiciary for sustainable follow-up

blocks.text: Public Interest Litigation has been India's moral revolution in law, transforming the judiciary from a passive arbiter to an active guardian of rights. Yet its legitimacy rests on judicial restraint, procedural discipline and civic sincerity.
